Title: Java4Shell Vulnerability: How Should Security Teams Identify and Reduce Exposure?
Context: Even after CVE-2026-114938 becomes available in Aquasec vulnerability feeds, detection coverage may vary depending on the Java distribution and package format
Full Text:
TL;DR: Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) is a high severity vulnerability affecting the OpenJDK HotSpot compiler, with a CVSS v3.1 score of 8.1. The published advisory identifies Java 17, 21, 25 and 27 release lines as affected, although exact vulnerable versions vary by distributor. Security teams should identify affected Java installations, prioritize production workloads and apply available security updates.

Aquasec expects CVE-2026-114938 to be available in its vulnerability feeds around 04:00 UTC on November 18, 2026 (Online CyberCenter) and 07:00 UTC on November 18, 2026 (Offline CyberCenter), after which customers can use native vulnerability scanning and Image Assurance Policies to identify images with matching findings.

What is the Java4Shell vulnerability?

Java4Shell, tracked as CVE-2026-114938, is a vulnerability in the OpenJDK HotSpot compiler, a component of the Java runtime responsible for compiling Java bytecode into native machine code during application execution.

The vulnerability carries a CVSS v3.1 score of 8.1 (High) and affects multiple supported OpenJDK release lines.

According to the published OpenJDK advisory, the following Java release lines are affected:

Java release line

Status

Java 17

Affected

Java 21

Affected

Java 25

Affected

Java 27

Affected

The exact affected and fixed builds depend on the Java distributor. Organizations should consult their distributor’s security advisory to determine whether their installed Java version is vulnerable and which update resolves the issue.

Why does Java4Shell matter to cloud native environments?

Java is widely used in enterprise applications, including services deployed in containers and Kubernetes environments. A vulnerability affecting the Java runtime can therefore create exposure across multiple applications even when their underlying application code has not changed.

In containerized environments, Java installations are frequently packaged directly into application images. Updating Java on the underlying host does not necessarily update the version embedded within those images. Organizations may need to rebuild and redeploy applications to remove vulnerable versions from production.

This creates an immediate challenge for security teams. They need to identify which container images contain affected Java versions, determine where those images are deployed and prioritize remediation based on the applications and services potentially exposed.

Why is vulnerability scanning alone insufficient to address Java4Shell?

Vulnerability scanning is essential for identifying affected Java installations, but its effectiveness depends on the availability and accuracy of vulnerability intelligence.

When a vulnerability is newly disclosed, there may be a delay before it becomes available in vulnerability feeds. During that period, a scan may not report the newly disclosed CVE even when an image contains an affected software version.

This is particularly relevant to Java4Shell because Aquasec expects CVE-2026-114938 to become available in its vulnerability feeds around 04:00 UTC on November 18, 2026 (Online CyberCenter) and 07:00 UTC on November 18, 2026 (Offline CyberCenter).

Security teams should therefore avoid treating the absence of a CVE finding as confirmation that an image is unaffected. Reviewing installed Java versions against distributor advisories remains important, particularly while vulnerability content is being updated.

Once the updated vulnerability information becomes available, organizations should rescan relevant images to identify matching findings and support remediation.

What does an effective Java4Shell response look like?

An effective response begins with identifying affected Java installations across container images and deployed applications.

Security teams should review the Java distributions and versions used throughout their environments, paying particular attention to images supporting internet facing or business critical applications.

Once affected images have been identified, organizations should update Java to the fixed version recommended by their distributor, rebuild the affected images and redeploy the corrected applications.

Teams should then rescan the updated images to confirm that the vulnerability finding has been resolved. This verification step is particularly important in containerized environments where older images may remain available in registries or continue to be deployed across multiple services.

How is Aquasec addressing Java4Shell?

Aquasec is updating its vulnerability feeds to include CVE-2026-114938, with availability expected around 04:00 UTC on November 18, 2026 (Online CyberCenter) and 07:00 UTC on November 18, 2026 (Offline CyberCenter).

Once the updated vulnerability content is available, customers can use native vulnerability scanning and Image Assurance Policies to identify container images with a matching CVE finding.

Customers can configure an Image Assurance Policy to evaluate images against CVE-2026-114938 using the built in CVEs Blocked control. A custom Rego check is not required for this workflow.

After the vulnerability content becomes available, customers should rescan relevant images, particularly those scanned before the update. They can then use Image Inventory to review images that failed the relevant policy and examine the associated vulnerability details, Java package and version, registry information and deployed workloads.

For customers using Image Assurance Policies for investigation, policy enforcement and CI/CD actions should be reviewed to avoid unintentionally blocking deployments or failing pipelines.

For detailed instructions, see the Aquasec Knowledge Base article on identifying affected Java4Shell images.

What should security teams know about Java4Shell detection results?

Even after CVE-2026-114938 becomes available in Aquasec vulnerability feeds, detection coverage may vary depending on the Java distribution and package format. A missing finding does not necessarily mean an image is unaffected. Organizations should verify their Java vendor and installed version against the appropriate security advisory, particularly when investigating images they believe may contain vulnerable software.

Similarly, an Image Assurance Policy failure does not automatically mean Java4Shell was detected. If the policy includes multiple controls, teams should review the specific failed check to confirm that CVE-2026-114938 triggered the result.

If a known affected image is not detected after the vulnerability content becomes available, customers should contact Aquasec Support for further investigation.

What should organizations do now to address Java4Shell?

Organizations should prioritize the following actions:

Identify affected Java installations. Review container images and deployed applications for Java 17, 21, 25 and 27, confirming the exact affected versions against the relevant distributor advisory.

Prioritize production exposure. Focus first on affected images supporting internet facing or business critical applications.

Apply available security updates. Update Java to the fixed version recommended by the distributor, then rebuild and redeploy affected container images.

Rescan when updated vulnerability content is available. Aquasec expects CVE-2026-114938 to be available in its vulnerability feeds around 04:00 UTC on November 18, 2026 (Online CyberCenter) and 07:00 UTC on November 18, 2026 (Offline CyberCenter).

Verify remediation. Confirm that corrected images are deployed and that the vulnerability finding has been resolved.

Once CVE-2026-114938 is available in Aqua’s vulnerability feeds, Aquasec customers can use native vulnerability scanning and Image Assurance Policies to identify affected images and verify remediation. Customers who believe a known affected image is not being detected should contact the Aquasec Support Portal for assistance.

Java4Shell reinforces the importance of maintaining accurate software inventories and responding quickly when new vulnerabilities are disclosed. While updated vulnerability intelligence supports more efficient identification, organizations should not delay reviewing affected Java versions or applying available security updates.

FAQs

What is CVE-2026-114938?

CVE-2026-114938, also known as Java4Shell, is a high severity vulnerability affecting the OpenJDK HotSpot compiler. It carries a CVSS v3.1 score of 8.1 and affects multiple Java release lines.

Which Java versions are affected by Java4Shell?

The published OpenJDK advisory identifies Java 17, 21, 25 and 27 release lines as affected. Exact vulnerable and fixed builds vary by distributor, so organizations should consult their Java vendor’s security advisory.

Can Aquasec detect Java4Shell?

Aquasec expects CVE-2026-114938 to become available in its vulnerability feeds around 04:00 UTC on November 18, 2026 (Online CyberCenter) and 07:00 UTC on November 18, 2026 (Offline CyberCenter). Once the updated content is available, customers can use native vulnerability scanning and Image Assurance Policies to identify images with matching CVE findings.

How can customers verify that Java4Shell remediation is complete?

Aquasec customers should update Java to the fixed version recommended by their distributor, rebuild and redeploy affected images, then rescan them using updated vulnerability content. They should also confirm that corrected images are deployed in production.

Does a missing Java4Shell finding mean an image is unaffected?

No. A missing finding does not confirm that an image is unaffected. Vulnerability content may not yet be available, and detection coverage can vary by Java distribution or package format. Organizations should verify installed Java versions against their distributor’s advisory.

Title: Uncovering GhostMap: The Rootkit Behind Shai-Hulud’s Rusty Cousin
Context: Watching only the installer’s child processes would therefore have missed the actual loader
Full Text:
How does IronWorm install and load GhostMap?

GhostMap runs as part of a larger implant. IronWorm handles installation, service persistence and collection; the rootkit provides concealment and anti-debugging. The sequence below follows the tested npm specimen from installation into those kernel mechanisms. It does not represent a complete infection followed through external command and control.

Figure 1. Two delivery channels with a shared execution pattern. In the compared payloads, installation creates a persistent service. The service loads the GhostMap rootkit component and operates the local collector. The detailed measurements below come from the IronWorm specimen.

Stage 1: IronWorm establishes persistence and loads GhostMap

JFrog documented a preinstall entry that invokes ./tools/setup during installation of [email protected] when lifecycle scripts are enabled. In the AUR channel, modified PKGBUILDs install atomic-lockfile, whose install hook executes its bundled Linux binary.

The npm page for [email protected] was marked as deprecated with the author message: “COMPROMISED via Mini Shai-Hulud worm (TeamPCP). Upgrade to latest.” This is the package author’s attribution in the warning; our analysis does not independently establish who developed or operated IronWorm. The screenshot documents deprecation, not removal from the registry.

Figure 2. Historical npm page screenshot showing the deprecation warning for [email protected] and its reference to Mini Shai-Hulud (TeamPCP).

Our runtime investigation began with the extracted executable, run with root privileges in the lab. In the initial runtime investigation, the specimen copied itself to /var/lib/glugi/glugi, created glugi.service and enabled the service. The executable started by systemd had the same hash as the original sample.

That successor process loaded GhostMap’s eBPF components. Watching only the installer’s child processes would therefore have missed the actual loader. Names varied across runs. One later installation used /var/lib/havebi/havebi. These paths are observed examples, not fixed names that every infection must use.

Stage 2: GhostMap attaches its eBPF programs to kernel events eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter) lets small programs run at defined points inside the Linux kernel. A program holds the logic; a hook is where it runs, such as a syscall exit. A link represents the attachment. A map stores data that programs consult or update, and a helper is a kernel function they can call under applicable restrictions.

GhostMap comprised 13 programs, 10 maps and 13 links at an active checkpoint in the IronWorm run. For process hiding, hidden_names holds selected process names. An execution hook can add matching processes to hidden_pids. Another map, scratch, temporarily records the address of a directory result buffer. For socket hiding, hidden_inodes stores socket inode identifiers, which the network concealment programs use to select entries.

Figure 3. Reconstructed terminal view of saved bpftool JSON, filtered for readability. On November 8, hidden_names selected dbus-daemon, hidden_pids held five PIDs and hidden_inodes held inode 23875. Memory evidence linked that inode to the listener on port 8738. Map IDs belong to this run.

Stage 3: GhostMap changes the answer delivered to the reader Linux exposes process information through /proc, a virtual filesystem. Its numeric directory names are process IDs (PIDs). The ps utility lists processes by reading this information.

A syscall is a request from an application to the kernel. The getdents64 syscall returns directory entries in a buffer in application memory. Each record contains a name and a length field, d_reclen, which tells the reader how far to advance to the next record.

GhostMap’s enter_getdents program remembers the buffer address. At sys_exit_getdents64, its exit_getdents program examines the returned records and checks numeric names against hidden_pids. When it finds a selected entry, it uses bpf_probe_write_user to modify the record chain. Increasing the preceding record’s length makes the reader advance past the hidden entry.

The saved map dumps make the selection concrete. We named benign test processes dbus-daemon to exercise the name matching. In the November 8 experiment, hidden_pids included benign test processes 3035 and 3934. Both disappeared from /proc enumeration while their known /proc/PID paths remained accessible. Control processes 3031 and 3930 were absent from the hiding map and remained listed. After the rootkit stopped, the hidden test processes became visible again.

Figure 4. Terminal reconstruction of a comparison computed from the same November 8 snapshots. Benign test PIDs 3035 and 3934 are in hidden_pids and missing from enumeration, but remain directly accessible and return after stopping the rootkit. Control PIDs 3031 and 3930 remain visible.

Hiding is not automatically inherited from a parent. A fork creates a child process; an exec loads a new program into a process. GhostMap’s on_exec hook checks the process’s short kernel name, comm, against hidden_names and adds a matching PID to hidden_pids. In our November 12 test, a fork-only child remained visible even though it inherited the name dbus-daemon. A child that executed a program with that name became hidden, even under a visible parent. A visible child with a parent missing from ps is therefore a useful hunting lead, but not proof of rootkit activity on its own.

Stage 4: One changed byte makes the reader skip a record In a separate experiment on November 10, we captured each directory buffer before GhostMap’s syscall exit hook and compared it with the same buffer delivered to a controlled reader. Matching the thread, buffer address and syscall interval let us identify precisely what changed.

In a controlled directory, the preceding record’s length changed from 32 to 56 bytes. The reader consequently skipped a file whose numeric name matched the hidden process’s PID. In /proc, a record length changed from 24 to 72 bytes, skipping the malware process and the hidden test process.

Each case reproduced three times. Across all six altered buffers, only one byte changed: the low byte of the two byte length field. The hidden records’ bytes remained in the buffer, and the syscall’s returned byte count stayed unchanged.

Figure 5. Terminal reconstruction displaying saved buffer measurements: the preceding record grows from 24 to 72 bytes, causing the reader to skip two PID entries.

The comparison stayed byte identical across 24 calls made before the rootkit started or after it stopped. Actual ps queries also omitted the hidden test process, both with and without our observer running. After the rootkit stopped, ps displayed the process again.

Figure 6. Reconstructed, filtered ps output from the November 10 experiment. While the rootkit is active, only control PID 3821 appears. After it stops, target PID 3820 appears too. The recorded command was ps -eo pid=; filtering was added for presentation. These PIDs belong to a separate run from Figures 3 and 4.

Stage 5: Socket concealment changes two different views Linux exposes socket information through more than one interface. /proc/net/tcp provides a text listing, while socket diagnostic requests over Netlink return structured messages that tools such as ss can interpret. GhostMap targets both paths.

In a separate listener experiment, GhostMap’s hidden_inodes map contained inode 18544, identifying IronWorm’s listener on 127.0.0.1:8738. This is a different run from Figure 3, where that listener had inode 23875; inode numbers are local to the observed socket instance. The listener disappeared from /proc/net/tcp in all three observations, while a benign listener on port 8739 remained visible.

The Netlink path produced a different result. GhostMap changed the listener’s diagnostic message type to NLMSG_NOOP, indicating a no-operation message, but left its port, identifier and listening state in the payload. The tested ss utility still displayed the listener in all three queries, although its process-owner annotation was absent. The corresponding upstream source provides a plausible explanation: its parsing path can read the retained payload without requiring the original message type.

The concealment code ran, but it did not hide the socket from that reader. The result applies to the tested ss package, iproute2 6.1.0-1ubuntu6.4; other consumers may handle the modified message differently.

Figure 7. Terminal reconstruction of the separate listener experiment: port 8738 is absent from /proc/net/tcp but visible to the tested ss utility; control port 8739 is visible in both. The hidden inode in this run was 18544, not the 23875 shown in Figure 3.

Title: Why Does AI Agent Security in Banking Require More Than Alerts?
Context: An agent can use legitimate credentials to create financial exposure without exploiting a vulnerability
Full Text:
TL;DR: AI agent security in banking requires controls that can deny prohibited workload actions before they complete, because an alert does not revoke an agent’s authority. An agent can use legitimate credentials to create financial exposure without exploiting a vulnerability. Aquasec combines deep runtime visibility with local enforcement through its full agent architecture, applying configured policies inside running workloads without waiting for centralized analysis. That control complements identity restrictions and transaction approvals, blocking supported operations that violate policy while the agent is executing.

What is the control gap in AI agent security?

Your bank’s exposure extends to the authority an agent’s workload gives it, which can be much broader than its assigned task. AI agent security must connect that task to enforceable limits on access and execution.

In Kubernetes, that authority can come from a service account, an associated cloud role, mounted credentials and available network paths. Instructions to inspect records do not remove credentials or close connections. A carefully written prompt therefore leaves the workload’s technical permissions unchanged. The agent can still attempt actions the business never intended it to take.

Why do internal AI agents require their own runtime controls?

Connecting an agent to production tools gives its decisions consequences inside your environment. A badly scoped instruction or a malicious prompt embedded in a document can lead it toward actions its existing access permits.

Blocking external agents at a customer login does nothing to constrain an internal agent using a workload identity. The bank still owns that exposure inside its clusters. Security cannot wait for a software exploit to establish that intervention is necessary, because an unwanted operation may use a valid credential and an allowed connection.

Where do access reviews and alerts fall short for AI agents?

Identity controls, image scanning and patching remain essential. They reduce unnecessary authority and address vulnerable software. A posture finding, however, leaves the identified access available until something changes it.

Adding runtime telemetry does not automatically close that gap. A sensor can observe an operation without being able to deny it locally. In a model that exports telemetry for centralized analysis and response, execution can continue while the decision is made.

For an agent connected to a financial system, that distinction is consequential. Investigating a completed operation and preventing that operation from completing produce different outcomes for the bank.

How should banks separate AI agent observation from action?

An agent assigned to inspect transactions should not automatically receive the authority to initiate them. Use dedicated identities and restrict available credentials to the resources its task requires. Require application approval for consequential operations, with read access limited to necessary records.

Then carry those boundaries into the running workload. Define the executable behavior and network destinations the task needs and enforce restrictions on supported operations outside that scope. The controls should hold when the agent misinterprets an instruction, without depending on the model to recognize its own mistake.

How does Aquasec enforce AI agent workload boundaries?

We put the enforcement decision inside the running workload through the Aquasec Enforcer. Our full agent architecture combines detailed runtime telemetry with local policy decisions at the kernel layer. In enforcement mode, it can deny supported operations that violate configured policy without waiting for centralized analysis or an analyst response.

Drift Prevention makes that distinction concrete. When an agent attempts to execute a binary introduced after deployment, the configured control can block execution. Network policies can also deny connections to prohibited destinations, restricting paths that the workload’s identity permissions might otherwise leave available.

Those controls act on the operation itself. Security teams get a way to constrain supported workload behavior while permissions are corrected, without making termination of the entire container the default response. Application authorization remains responsible for deciding which transactions an agent may perform.

How do AI agent security approaches compare at execution?

Evaluate what happens to the attempted operation. The comparison below separates finding driven posture from telemetry led detection without local enforcement. Aquasec entries assume supported controls configured for enforcement.

Dimension

Traditional approach

Modern approach

Aquasec approach

Primary function

Identify excessive access

Detect workload behavior

Enforce workload policy

Decision path

Remediation workflow

Central analysis and response

Local enforcement

Evidence

The architectural distinction is whether the security component can apply the restriction inside the workload, without waiting for a separate response workflow.

How can an AI agent create financial exposure without an exploit?

Valid access can turn a poorly scoped task into an unintended transaction.

Example: A reconciliation agent is asked to resolve a failed settlement. Its workload holds a payment credential and can reach an internal transfer service. Without a separate approval check, it could attempt the settlement again from another funding account. Every step can use an allowed operation.

This hypothetical scenario explains the exposure; it is not a reported customer incident or a measured product result. The missing boundary is between the assigned task and the authority available to complete it.

What mistakes weaken AI agent workload controls?

Exceptions can reopen the access a runtime policy was intended to restrict. Do not approve broad exceptions just to remove a block. Validate the required dependency and limit the exception to what the application needs.

Do not treat a permitted connection as transaction approval. If read and transfer operations share the same allowed service, the application must authorize them separately. Workload network restrictions do not determine whether an individual financial transaction is legitimate.

What should banks demand from AI agent security next?

Banks should make demonstrated enforcement a condition of expanding AI agent access. Before giving an agent greater authority, require evidence that the controls protecting its workload can stop the prohibited behavior they are designed to address. An alert that leaves the operation untouched does not meet that standard.

We put that enforcement inside the running workload through the Aquasec Enforcer. Our full agent architecture combines deep runtime visibility with local policy enforcement, allowing configured controls to block supported operations without waiting for centralized analysis or an analyst response. That gives banks a way to restrict what an agent’s workload can execute, alongside the identity and application controls governing its access

FAQ

How does Aquasec differentiate AI agent security from runtime monitoring?

Aquasec combines runtime telemetry with local policy enforcement through a full agent architecture. For supported operations in enforcement mode, the workload does not need to wait for centralized analysis before a configured restriction can deny the action.

Can AI agent security stop misuse of valid credentials?

Aquasec can deny supported workload operations that violate configured policy even when credentials are available. A request that remains permitted still needs authorization and any required approval within the application.

Does this AI agent security strategy cover externally hosted agents?

Aquasec enforcement applies to supported workloads where it is deployed. Protecting a bank’s clusters does not automatically protect agents running on laptops or external platforms. Those deployments require their own access controls.

Title: Integrate Aquasec and Jenkins to Stop Unsafe Images Before They Run
Context: How does the Aquasec and Jenkins integration work
Full Text:
How does the Aquasec and Jenkins integration work?

The Aqua Security Scanner plugin is installed from the central Jenkins plugin repository, or deployed manually from its .hpi file. It is configured under Manage Jenkins, System, in the Aqua Security section. There an administrator sets the Aquasec scanner image, the Aquasec server URL and a scanner token. Both values come from the deployment command of a CI/CD scanner group. Aquasec SaaS accepts token authentication only, so username and password authentication is not an option for SaaS environments.

The plugin works in Pipeline and Freestyle jobs. In a pipeline, the aqua step goes into the pipeline script, and the Jenkins Snippet Generator can build the syntax. With the Docker engine, the plugin scans local images, images hosted in a registry and docker-archive tar files. With Podman, supported from plugin version 3.1.2, it scans local images as a root or non root user.

Each job chooses what happens to a noncompliant image: never fail the build, or perform the actions defined in the Image Assurance Policy. Local images and archives are evaluated against the Default Image Assurance Policy. Registry images are evaluated against every policy whose scope includes them. Optional settings register the image with Aquasec after a successful scan, hide base image vulnerabilities and run a shell command when an image fails.

Results appear in Jenkins as an Aquasec scan report organized like the image view in the Aquasec UI. A View in Aqua Platform button opens the image under Workload Protection, Images & Functions, Images, CI/CD Scans. A separate Aqua Security Serverless Scanner plugin scans function code for vulnerabilities, sensitive data and excessive permissions.

Title: Integrate Aquasec and Prometheus for Greater Visibility Into Runtime Security Operations
Context: Platform Aqua Platform Runtime Powered Cloud Security Monitor behavior, detect exploitable risk, enforce policy and contain threats across the application lifecycle
Full Text:
How does the Aquasec and Prometheus integration work?

The integration uses two separate configurations to make diagnostic metrics available to Prometheus.

Aquasec Platform monitoring

Administrators enable Prometheus under Administration, Integrations, Monitoring Systems in the Aquasec Platform.

The configuration supports an optional bearer token and a configurable data collection interval. Aquasec makes diagnostic metrics available at the specified interval, including the number of connected Enforcers and Gateways, images waiting to be scanned, images being scanned and images that failed scanning.

The integration also provides metrics for successful and failed user logins, defined Image Assurance Policies, Runtime Policies and Firewall Policies.

These metrics help teams understand the operational state of their Aquasec environment and identify patterns that may require attention.

Aquasec Enforcer monitoring

For more detailed runtime monitoring, Aquasec provides a Prometheus Metrics Exporter for Aquasec Enforcers and VM Enforcers.

Administrators enable the exporter under Settings, Enforcer, Prometheus Metrics Exporter. The exporter uses port 8995 by default, although this can be changed. The Metrics Exporter advanced setting must also be enabled for the relevant Enforcer groups.

The exporter exposes several categories of metrics, including:

Resource utilization: CPU and memory usage at the host and Enforcer levels, helping teams monitor the resources consumed by runtime protection.

Enforcer health: Enforcer version and type, active container counts, enabled functions and Gateway connection status.

Runtime security activity: File related events detected or blocked by runtime controls, malware scanning activity and behavioral detection event counts.

Security operations: Audit activity, event processing errors and host or image scanning results.

For Kubernetes deployments, Aquasec’s documentation provides an example using a local Prometheus server with service discovery to collect metrics within a cluster. A remote Prometheus server can use federation to collect metrics across clusters. Standalone Aquasec Enforcers and VM Enforcers do not require the local cluster deployment step.

This architecture allows organizations to monitor Aquasec metrics across distributed environments while maintaining the runtime enforcement capabilities that operate inside protected workloads.

Title: HTTP2Shell Vulnerability: How Should Security Teams Assess and Reduce Exposure?
Context: Aqua Team October 27, 2026 Updated: October 29th, 2026 TL;DR: The HTTP2Shell vulnerability (CVE-2026-111497) is a critical flaw in Google’s Brotli decompression decoder that...
Full Text:
How is Aquasec addressing HTTP2Shell?

Aquasec has reviewed the impact of HTTP2Shell on its own components and confirmed that the affected Brotli library was present in certain Aquasec Enforcer images.

However, our security analysis determined that the vulnerable decoding functionality is not used by Enforcer components. The Enforcer does not decompress Brotli data, meaning the conditions required to exploit HTTP2Shell through the affected decoder are not present in the assessed Enforcer execution paths.

Our assessment included examination of both source code and released binaries to verify that the vulnerable decoder is not invoked during Enforcer operation.

Although the vulnerable library was not reachable through Enforcer functionality, we have released an updated Enforcer versions for both Update 47 and Update 45 LTS containing the corrected Brotli package.

Aquasec Enforcer 2022.4 U47 SP2 (2022.4.951.5) and 2022.4 U45 Enforcer LTS SP9 (2022.4.880.50) are now available. We recommend that customers upgrade to this release to remove the vulnerable dependency and address associated scanner findings.

Customers looking for additional information about affected versions, our technical assessment and upgrade guidance can refer to the Aquasec Support Knowledge Base and the U47 SP2 release documentation or the U45 Enforcer LTS SP9 release documentation

Title: PHP2Shell: How to Protect Vulnerable PHP Workloads While Patching
Context: Aquasec provides vulnerability detection and runtime controls to help identify exposure and restrict supported unauthorized activities while customers apply security updates
Full Text:
How does Aquasec protect PHP workloads?

Aquasec enforces security policies inside running workloads, allowing security teams to restrict supported unauthorized actions without depending exclusively on vulnerability specific signatures.

Four runtime control areas are particularly relevant to PHP workloads.

Restrict unauthorized process execution. Runtime policies can restrict PHP workloads from launching unnecessary shells and download utilities such as `sh`, `bash`, `curl` and `wget`. This can interrupt certain attempts to execute additional commands or retrieve malicious payloads.

Prevent unauthorized executable changes. Aquasec Drift Prevention can block execution of executable files that were not present in the original container image. This helps restrict newly introduced malicious binaries, although it does not independently prevent a PHP script from running through the existing interpreter.

Restrict unauthorized network activity. Appropriate runtime network controls can restrict unnecessary outbound connections and help limit certain reverse shell activities or communication with attacker controlled infrastructure.

Protect application files. File integrity monitoring can detect unauthorized modifications to sensitive application directories. File modification restrictions can prevent changes when properly configured, including changes to PHP web roots where malicious scripts might be introduced.

The effectiveness of these controls depends on workload coverage, policy configuration and the attack technique. In enforcement mode, validated policies can block supported unauthorized actions. They should not be represented as complete protection against either PHP2Shell vulnerability, particularly the reported memory disclosure path.

Title: How Do Financial Institutions Measure and Control Cyber Risk?
Context: Identify available policies that are not enforced, test relevant attack paths and document coverage and exceptions
Full Text:
What do financial regulations require institutions to demonstrate about cybersecurity controls?

Across five major regulatory regimes, financial institutions are expected to demonstrate effective management of technology risk and operational resilience. The requirements differ by jurisdiction, but they share an emphasis on accountable management, appropriate controls and evidence that those controls work.

United States: NYDFS Part 500 NYDFS Part 500 connects cybersecurity safeguards with executive accountability. For covered entities subject to the relevant provisions, annual submissions must be supported by evidence of material compliance or an acknowledgment identifying noncompliance and remediation. The regulation also addresses vulnerability management, access controls and tested incident response and recovery.

Runtime evidence can contribute to that record when it shows how an applicable control operated.

Canada: OSFI OSFI B-13 sets expectations for technology and cyber risk management, including control testing, asset inventories, preventive defenses and recovery.

E-21 connects that work to critical operations, dependencies, disruption tolerances and scenario testing. Full adherence was expected by September 1, 2026, with scenario testing for all critical operations to be completed by September 1, 2027. B-10 retains the institution’s accountability for third party arrangements.

A blocked container action becomes more useful when the institution can connect it to the critical operation it protects.

European Union: DORA DORA places ultimate responsibility for ICT risk with the management body. Its requirements cover ICT risk management, incident reporting, resilience testing and third party risk.

For financial entities subject to Article 24, appropriate tests must cover ICT systems and applications supporting critical or important functions at least annually. Control results should therefore inform remediation and the wider assessment of operational resilience.

Singapore: MAS MAS combines binding technology risk and cyber hygiene notices with supervisory guidance on technology risk, outsourcing and business continuity. For banks, the relevant notices are FSM-N05 and FSM-N06.

MAS emphasizes recoverable critical IT systems, customer information protection and critical business services with external dependencies.

A consultation on further technology risk management notice amendments ran from June 10 to July 31, 2026. Those proposals should be distinguished from requirements already in force.

Australia: APRA The Australian Prudential Regulation Authority places control effectiveness and operational resilience under board oversight.

CPS 234 requires information security controls proportionate to the information assets they protect, with systematic testing of effectiveness. CPS 230 connects operational risk to critical operations, disruption tolerances, tested continuity plans and oversight of material service providers.

For a payment service, runtime test results can help demonstrate which supporting workloads are protected, alongside evidence that the service can continue or recover within its tolerances.
